seed_question: Does encoding a language model's competing claims as an entangled quantum state flag its wrong answers better than classical controls?
note: Structure and open paths only. Where a node lists bets, its verdict, odds and dates come from ledger/bets.jsonl, never from this file. Phase A nodes (before the ledger began) carry their outcome here, taken from entangled-mind paper/record.md. directions.title: H1: does the encoding faithfully hold the model's claims?
directions.closed_line: 2026-11-05 remap: H1 (the encoding faithfully holds the claims) was the gate for H2-H4, which were all killed; CONTEXT.md §3 rule 6 forbids reviving the quantum error-prediction encoding, so no follow-up may grow from it.

directions.title: H2, the primary: does the entangled readout flag the model's wrong answers?
directions.diagnosis: The entangled readout did worse than every classical control (AUROC 0.55 against 0.64–0.68), and noise is not the cause.
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku's claims in program 1's set, an entangled readout of competing claims flagging wrong answers better than classical controls (0.55 against 0.64-0.68).

directions.title: H3 and H4: do the entanglement and the relation web carry information?
directions.diagnosis: Both falsified. The real relation web scored below 99% of 200 shuffled webs.
directions.rules_out: Rules out, in this encoding, the entangling gates or the real relation web carrying the error signal: the real web scored below 99% of shuffled webs.

directions.title: H5: do the entangled states survive real quantum hardware?
directions.result: Entanglement certified on 3 of 3 items on ibm_fez (46 QPU s).

directions.title: Does the model's own stated confidence carry the error signal?
directions.result: Stated confidence (0.82) beat every structural arm.

directions.title: Does a learned quantum encoding beat a matched classical twin?
directions.diagnosis: A tie, 0.83 against 0.84. The fit set the couplings near zero: it switched entanglement off itself.
directions.rules_out: Rules out a learned quantum encoding beating its matched classical twin on Haiku's errors (0.83 against 0.84); the fit switched entanglement off by itself.

directions.title: Does an honest-hedge encoding help?
directions.diagnosis: Not met, 0.84 against 0.82. The hedge weight fitted to zero; the hedge was not the problem.
directions.rules_out: Rules out the honest-hedge term as the missing ingredient of the quantum encoding: its weight fitted to zero.

directions.title: Is the edge on Sonnet's errors entanglement?
directions.diagnosis: No. The edge is a per-claim readout angle; a classical twin matches it exactly and setting couplings to zero changes nothing.
directions.rules_out: Rules out entanglement as the source of the edge on Sonnet's errors: a per-claim readout angle carries it, and a classical twin matches it exactly.

directions.title: Experiment 3: do quantum or classical predictions track yes/no order effects?
directions.diagnosis: Inconclusive. The model is near-deterministic: 85% of items give the same answer in all five runs.
directions.rules_out: Rules out nothing about order effects on yes/no answers: the model gave the same answer in all five runs on 85% of items, so there was nothing to move.

directions.title: Experiment 4: do the model's ratings follow the Yearsley–Trueblood quantum rules?
directions.result: Conjunction fallacies on 7 of 16 items and order effects of about +0.10, but the mechanism is undetermined.

directions.title: Anchoring or content-driven updating, with a provided first rating?
directions.diagnosis: Untestable. The model resists a first rating it is given: in 15 of 32 item-orders it never accepted one.
directions.rules_out: Rules out a provided first rating as a usable anchoring manipulation on Haiku: it never accepted one in 15 of 32 item-orders.

directions.title: Experiment 5: does a quantum belief state predict sequential ratings better than a matched classical updater?
directions.diagnosis: A tie. A dephased classical Markov chain matches the quantum state; no QQ or Kvam signature.
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on experiment 5's items, a quantum belief state predicting sequential ratings better than a dephased classical Markov chain; no QQ or Kvam signature.

directions.title: Are the graded order effects real, on one scale direction?
directions.result: Yes: a median 25-point swing, surviving one scale direction (12 of 16 large pairs). The live finding grew from here.

directions.title: Gold map 9: clonable minds. Does asking an earlier question change later answers?
directions.novelty_line: That earlier turns shift a model's later judgments is in print: Temkit (2026, arXiv:2605.22714) finds binary verdicts drift toward planted prior answers across 12 models including Anthropic Haiku through Opus (d = -0.17), and Simhi et al. (2026, arXiv:2603.03308, ICML) report prior turns biasing later responses in three model families. Kang (2026, arXiv:2607.17219) audits question order with committed answers but found saturated outputs. None states our result: 0-100 ratings moving 12 to 23 points after the model's own earlier questions, read as no-signalling-in-time invasiveness, nor the null for a midway yes/no choice (no LLM replication of Kvam et al. 2015 found). Search: WebSearch for "no-signalling in time", "Leggett-Garg", "macrorealism", "question order effects" and "Kvam interference choice confidence" with "language model" or "LLM", then the arXiv abstract page of each hit.

directions.title: Gold map 2: is the order effect the question, or the model seeing its own answers?
directions.novelty_line: That hiding the model's earlier answer makes it repeat itself far less is in print: Kumaran et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.03120) found hiding the initial answer roughly triples change of mind. That the order of the questions still moves the final rating when the answers are hidden is not: AMEL (Temkit 2026, arXiv 2605.22714) and Kang 2026 (arXiv 2607.17219) measure history and order effects with the answers visible, and Huang et al. (COLM 2026, arXiv 2602.24287) drop assistant turns without measuring order. Ours is the only test found where the questions stay and the answers go; its weaknesses are its own (10 items, two carrying most of the effect, and a "[rating recorded]" placeholder the follow-up gm2-f1 removes). Search: paper/novelty.md, 2026-11-05 (arXiv searches on question-order effects in LLMs, accumulated message effects, redacted or hidden assistant turns), by a claude-fable-5-1 session on the novelty-check branch (93f47af); carried here by the informed-engine session.

directions.title: Robustness: direction 2 on all 40 experiment-5 items
directions.novelty_line: The 40-item replication of em-gm2, with the same standing against the literature: the visible-answer part (repeat agreement falls when the earlier answer is hidden) is Kumaran et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.03120); the order effect surviving with the answers hidden (ratio 1.23 [0.75, 2.02] here) is not stated in AMEL (Temkit 2026, arXiv 2605.22714), Kang 2026 (arXiv 2607.17219) or Huang et al. (COLM 2026, arXiv 2602.24287), all of which keep the answers visible or measure no order. Partly new, with the same placeholder confound as em-gm2. Search: paper/novelty.md, 2026-11-05, by a claude-fable-5-1 session on the novelty-check branch (93f47af); carried here by the informed-engine session.

directions.title: Multi-model: shown / redacted / planted transcripts on Sonnet and Opus
directions.novelty_line: The multi-model run of em-gm2 (mixed: Sonnet's order effect survives redaction, ratio 2.95 [0.99, 12.55]; Opus's does not decide, 0.93 [0.06, 7.31]). The prior work is em-gm2's: the visible-answer part is Kumaran et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.03120, on Gemma 3, GPT-4o and o1-preview); no paper found measures the order effect with the answers hidden on any model, so the Sonnet and Opus readings have no prior statement either way. Search: paper/novelty.md, 2026-11-05, by a claude-fable-5-1 session on the novelty-check branch (93f47af); carried here by the informed-engine session.

directions.title: Gold map 3: is there a credence at all? Six elicitation formats
directions.novelty_line: Smolin and Wilder (2026, arXiv:2609.07943) fit one latent belief to 16 prompts on nine models (Gemma 3, Llama 3.1 70B, Qwen3 32B, DeepSeek V3.2, GLM-5, GPT-5.6; no Claude) and find it reconstructs behaviour well only for the most capable, with weaker models showing framing effects and "monotonic but weak and noisy" links. Lu et al. (2025, arXiv:2504.19445) and Pawitan and Holmes (2024, arXiv:2412.15296) also report format-dependent or incoherent judgments. None states our result: on Claude Haiku's own claims, six formats disagree beyond any monotone lens, with rank reversals on 12 to 25% of pairs and a separate-belief model winning on 86% of claims. Search: WebSearch for "elicitation format", "latent belief", "credence", "betting odds", "yes/no versus rating" with "LLM", 2025 to 2026; arXiv abstract pages and the Smolin and Wilder PDF opened.

directions.title: Free look: does the scale-direction gap predict errors?
directions.rules_out: Rules out the gap between the two scale directions as an error signal on Haiku: the 37-point gap does not track its errors (AUROC 0.48).

directions.short: Predict a format from the others
directions.title: Robustness: predict each format from the other five
directions.novelty_line: Predicting a held-out prompt from the others is Smolin and Wilder's (2026, arXiv:2609.07943) own test: on nine non-Claude models they report held-out R2 of 60 to 90% for capable models, pooled R2 of about 0.6 to 0.8 zero-shot to an unseen framing, and much lower scores for less capable models. Our figure for Claude Haiku on its own claims is an R2 of 0.37 from the other five formats, or 39% of each format's split-half ceiling, below their range; the ceiling-normalised ratio appears nowhere we found. Search: WebSearch for "latent belief" "held-out" "framing" "LLM" and "cross-format prediction credence"; Smolin and Wilder PDF read in full.

directions.title: Multi-model: six formats on Sonnet and Opus
directions.novelty_line: That a single-belief description fits more capable models better is already stated by Smolin and Wilder (2026, arXiv:2609.07943): held-out fit rises along a capability gradient and framing effects are "largely absent in the strongest models"; their nine models include no Claude. Our Claude-family gradient (Haiku +19.4, Sonnet +9.2, Opus +1.9 per claim; Kendall's W 0.54, 0.71, 0.87) points the same way, but the held-out-repeat comparison across Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, Sonnet's mixed reading and Opus's near-agreement on the project's own claims are not in print. Search: WebSearch for "latent belief" "capability" "framing effects" "LLM" and "Claude Haiku Sonnet Opus elicitation format"; Smolin and Wilder PDF read in full.

directions.title: Calibration (ECE) under two formats and two question orders
directions.novelty_line: That verbalised-confidence ECE depends on how the question is asked is in print: Tian et al. (2023, arXiv:2305.14975, EMNLP) report claude-2 ECE from 0.048 to 0.238 across their prompt variants on SciQ, and Kim and Kang (2026, arXiv:2605.27752) call confidence "protocol-dependent" on open models, most of the shift coming from the instruction. A 2026 preprint (arXiv:2603.01239) finds Claude Sonnet 4.6's calibration error drifting across turns. None tests probability against frequency wording (a human precedent is Gigerenzer and Hoffrage, 1995, Psychological Review), finds a format effect on Sonnet but not Haiku, or reports a question-order null. Search: WebSearch for "verbalized confidence" with "frequency format", "out of 100", "question order", "multi-turn calibration ECE"; arXiv abstract pages opened and Tian et al. HTML read.

directions.title: Gold map 1: does a model know its own errors better than another model reading the same answer?
directions.rules_out: Rules out privileged self-knowledge of errors for Haiku in this 2x2: Sonnet, reading Haiku's answers, spots Haiku's errors better than Haiku does.

directions.title: Multi-model: self-knowledge with Sonnet and Opus judging each other
directions.rules_out: Rules out a self-knowledge advantage on a second model pair: Opus judges Sonnet's errors better than Sonnet does.

directions.title: Gold map 4: does the model seek the evidence that would settle its own conflict?
directions.novelty_line: Jhaveri et al. 2026 (arXiv 2604.02485) report that eleven LLMs in a Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery game mostly propose tests that confirm their current hypothesis rather than falsify it, and Bertolazzi et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.04751) find the models that do seek falsification succeed more. Neither scores tests by expected information gain, shows the model a menu of its own claims about its own answer, or tests a Claude model. Our Haiku result agrees in lean (confirmatory) but is undecided on the informative-versus-confirmatory comparison, which is not in print: partly new. Search: WebSearch for "Jhaveri confirmation bias LLM", "LLM expected information gain choose question", "LLM self-verification evidence selection", "Wason 2-4-6 LLM information gain"; arXiv abstract and HTML pages opened.

directions.title: Gold map 5: does an internal truth probe on an open model hold still while question order moves the words?
directions.novelty_line: Schouten et al. 2024/2025 (arXiv 2404.18865, COLM 2025) report that truth probes are context sensitive and that preceding sentences which should not change a statement's truth still shift probe outputs; Adarsh et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.06599, ACL 2026) report that added context rotates and rescales the true-versus-false direction, more so when it conflicts with stored knowledge. Neither varies the order of prior sub-questions, sizes the shift against the probe's own true-false gap, or compares it with the verbal rating's shift; our 6% figure on Llama-3-8B and the undetermined probe-rating tracking are not in print: partly new. Search: WebSearch for "truth probe sensitivity to context", "sycophancy probe internal truth representation", "truth direction geometry context ACL 2026"; arXiv abstracts of the leads and hits opened.

directions.title: Gold map 6: does representation geometry predict order-effect size?
directions.question: When two questions sit close together inside the model, does asking them in a different order move its answers more?
known: Order really does move the model's ratings: a median 25-point swing on one scale.
Our own encoder's geometry failed to predict where order effects appear (1 win, 2 losses); the model's own was never measured.
directions.cheapest_test: On an open model, measure how close about 100 claim pairs sit internally, and check whether that predicts each pair's order effect better than a simple anchoring rule.
directions.odds_event: Internal overlap predicts the size of the order effect beyond the classical anchoring predictor.
directions.prior_work_line: No prior statement found after searching arXiv and the repo's reads for internal representation overlap predicting question-order effect size in a language model. Nearest: Lo, Sadrzadeh and Mansfield 2024 (arXiv:2412.16806, BERT) found Euclidean embedding distance the best predictor of CbD contextuality, with closer words more contextual; that is contextuality, not order-effect size, and has no anchoring baseline. Not on a Claude model.
prior_work_sources: Lo, Sadrzadeh, Mansfield 2024, Quantum-Like Contextuality in Large Language Models, arXiv:2412.16806
Riechers, Elliott, Shai 2025, Neural networks leverage nominally quantum and post-quantum representations, arXiv:2507.07432
Park et al. 2023, The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of LLMs, arXiv:2311.03658 (unverified, cited from gold-map.md)
directions.prior_work_search: arXiv abstracts of the gold-map citations; WebSearch 'representation overlap predicts question order effect LLM' returned nothing direct

directions.title: Gold map 10: post-quantum belief geometry on natural text, or contextuality at scale
directions.question: Are the model's beliefs stored in a shape that ordinary probability cannot describe?
known: Our graded ratings show almost no contextuality: 1 pair in 80; another study also found none.
Networks trained on toy processes show quantum-like belief shapes; natural text is untested.
directions.cheapest_test: Look at the internal belief geometry of an open model on natural text and test whether it falls outside the ordinary probability shape.
directions.odds_event: Natural-text belief states lie outside the classical probability simplex.
directions.prior_work_line: Mixed. Riechers, Elliott and Shai 2025 (arXiv:2507.07432) report transformers and RNNs representing beliefs over quantum and post-quantum generative models of their training data, which predicts a pass if natural text has such structure; Levinson 2026 (arXiv:2604.02685) looked for belief geometry in Gemma-2-9B on natural text and found only classical simplices, five candidate clusters, preliminary. Neither is a Claude model; neither tests the simplex-exclusion rule.
prior_work_sources: Riechers, Elliott, Shai 2025, Neural networks leverage nominally quantum and post-quantum representations, arXiv:2507.07432
Levinson 2026, Finding Belief Geometries with Sparse Autoencoders, arXiv:2604.02685
Kumar, Flint, Aiello, Baronchelli 2026, Failure of contextual invariance in large language models, arXiv:2603.23485
directions.prior_work_search: arXiv abstracts of the gold-map citations

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.0/3.1: does a number pull harder when framed as the model's own earlier answer?
directions.novelty_line: Kumaran and colleagues (Google DeepMind, July 2025, arXiv 2507.03120; Nature Machine Intelligence 2026) found that seeing its own earlier answer raised a model's confidence in it by 0.21 and cut its change-of-mind rate from 32.5% (hidden) to 13.1% (shown), while the same visible answer attributed to another model made no difference (31.3% against 33.2%), on Gemma 3 12B, GPT-4o and o1-preview; they call it a drive for self-consistency. Ours is the same result as a numeric slope on a Claude model (own +0.42 of the way, other +0.05), with the two conditions also differing in wording: a clean replication on a new family, worth one line and no more. Search: paper/novelty.md, 2026-11-05 (arXiv searches on LLM self-consistency, own-answer anchoring, change of mind under criticism), by a claude-fable-5-1 session on the novelty-check branch (93f47af); carried here by the informed-engine session.

directions.title: Source × distance × lag: does own-over-other hold at other distances and after a delay?
directions.novelty_line: The source part is in print: Kumaran et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.03120) find Gemma 3, GPT-4o and o1-preview change their mind far less when their own initial answer is visible (13.1% against 32.5% hidden) and that the effect disappears when the same answer is attributed to another LLM (33.2% against 31.3%). Their design is two turns at one fixed foil separation, so neither the fall in uptake with distance (0.71, 0.44, 0.21 at 10, 30, 60 points) nor the survival of the pull across three filler turns is stated there or anywhere else found: partly new. Search: WebSearch for "LLM anchoring own prior answer versus other", "LLM anchoring anchor distance extreme anchors", "LLM anchoring persists across intervening turns", "serial dependence large language models"; arXiv abstracts and the Kumaran HTML (both halves) opened.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.1: confidence-gated confirmation toward another person's number
directions.rules_out: Rules out confidence-gated confirmation on Haiku's run-3 calls: another person's estimate was taken up no more when it agreed with Haiku's side.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.10: does the next rating move toward or away from the last number?
directions.novelty_line: That numbers already in an LLM's context pull its next rating toward them is in print: Stureborg et al. 2024 (arXiv 2405.01724) find GPT-4's own earlier coherence score raises its later consistency score, Kapetanovic et al. 2026 (arXiv 2608.25869) find a shown prior score shifts judge ratings toward its value (d up to 0.71), and Temkit 2026 (arXiv 2605.22714) finds history polarity drags judgments its way across 12 models including Claude Haiku (d = -0.22). None holds the content's logical push fixed, tests a sub-question-then-main-question pair, or pits assimilation against contrast as we do: partly new. Search: WebSearch for "LLM sequential ratings assimilation serial dependence", "LLM-as-judge prior score anchoring", "LLM survey question order assimilation contrast"; arXiv abstracts and the Stureborg HTML opened; Fischer and Whitney and Cicchini via Europe PMC.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.4: is the model sampling probabilities (PT+N identity)?
directions.rules_out: Rules out probability-plus-noise sampling as the source of Haiku's conjunction fallacies on these 16 vignettes: Z sits near zero with no item-level slope.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.5: do serial-position weights rule out competing accumulators (LCA)?
directions.rules_out: Rules out a competing-accumulator U-shape in serial-position weights on these chains; the final verdict barely tracks the sub-ratings just given.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.3: precision weighting (predictive coding)
directions.question: Does a hint about base rates move the model's shaky beliefs more than its confident ones?
known: Stated confidence carries the error signal as well as any structural model (0.82 to 0.91).
The brain theory behind this (precision weighting) is a simulation, with no data of its own.
directions.cheapest_test: Rate the 160 claims under two base-rate hints, ten repeats each, and check whether the shift is bigger where stated confidence is low.
directions.prior_work_line: Owusu and Feldman 2026 (ACL short, doi:10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16; Llama and Qwen, not Claude) found anchoring susceptibility negatively correlated with model confidence regardless of accuracy, and larger for high anchors; this predicts a pass (base-rate hints move low-confidence claims more), with the risk that confidence there was distributional, not stated. Feldman and Friston 2010 (doi:10.3389/fnhum.2010.00215) is a simulation with no data.
prior_work_sources: Owusu, Feldman 2026, Anchoring Depends on Confidence and Post-Training in Language Models, ACL 2026 short papers, doi:10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16
Feldman, Friston 2010, Attention, uncertainty, and free-energy, Front. Hum. Neurosci. 4:215, doi:10.3389/fnhum.2010.00215
directions.prior_work_search: ACL Anthology abstract of Owusu and Feldman; biomimetic-map.md read of Feldman and Friston

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.6: bounded accumulation and 2DSD
directions.question: Does the model's confidence keep improving after it has already given its answer?
known: Making a choice midway did not change later confidence (no human-sized effect).
People's confidence keeps building after a choice; the published prediction here is not unique.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask the model to reconsider, or give it a filler task, after its answer, and check whether its confidence tracks the truth better.
directions.prior_work_line: Mixed. Human 2DSD (Pleskac and Busemeyer 2007 CogSci precursor, read in the repo; the 2010 Psych. Rev. paper, doi:10.1037/a0019737, unverified) predicts post-choice accumulation sharpens confidence. On LLMs, CritiCal (Zong et al. 2025, arXiv:2510.24505) reports that plain self-critique, the model reconsidering and revising its confidence, is beaten by trained critique and gives limited gains; Huang et al. 2023 (arXiv:2310.01798) found unaided self-correction worsens answers. No Claude data on the pass rule.
prior_work_sources: Pleskac, Busemeyer 2010, Two-stage dynamic signal detection, Psych. Rev. 117:864, doi:10.1037/a0019737 (unverified; 2007 CogSci precursor read per biomimetic-map.md)
Zong et al. 2025, CritiCal: Can Critique Help LLM Uncertainty or Confidence Calibration?, arXiv:2510.24505
Huang et al. 2023, Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, arXiv:2310.01798
directions.prior_work_search: WebSearch 'LLM confidence calibration after reconsideration self-reflection AUROC'; arXiv abstract of CritiCal; PubMed and PsycNet for Pleskac 2010 did not load

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.7: second-order metacognition (Fleming & Daw)
directions.question: After the model commits to an answer, does its confidence get better at telling right from wrong?
known: The other half of this theory already failed: choosing did not lower later confidence.
The 450 conversations with and without a choice are archived, so this costs nothing.
directions.cheapest_test: Using the archived conversations, compare how well the final rating separates true from false answers with a choice made versus without.
directions.odds_event: The final rating's AUROC is higher with a midway choice (K1) than without (K0).
directions.prior_work_line: Human theory and data predict a pass. Fleming and Daw 2017 (doi:10.1037/rev0000045, Fig. 6) predict a committed choice raises metacognitive sensitivity while lowering confidence; Siedlecka, Paulewicz and Wierzchon 2016 (doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00218, 86 people, anagrams) found confidence given after the response tracked accuracy better than confidence given before (slope difference z = 2.78, p = 0.003). No LLM or Claude statement found for AUROC after a midway choice.
prior_work_sources: Fleming, Daw 2017, Self-evaluation of decision-making: a general Bayesian framework for metacognitive computation, Psych. Rev. 124:91, doi:10.1037/rev0000045
Siedlecka, Paulewicz, Wierzchon 2016, But I Was So Sure! Metacognitive Judgments Are Less Accurate Given Prospectively than Retrospectively, Front. Psychol. 7:218, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00218
directions.prior_work_search: biomimetic-map.md full read of Fleming and Daw; Frontiers full text of Siedlecka 2016; WebSearch for an LLM version returned nothing

directions.odds_template: v1
directions.title: Belief survives forgetting: after a fine-tune makes an open model forget its true/false answers, does a truth probe trained before the fine-tune still read the truth?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: random-label LoRA should push verbal accuracy to chance; a frozen layer-13 probe starting at 0.86-1.00 probably stays above 0.80; the main risk is that verbal AUROC from logits survives a one-answer bias and erases the 0.15 margin; 4-bit is a further risk.
directions.cost: $0 API; laptop ~4-6 h (MLX LoRA on Llama-3-8B-4bit)
directions.assumption_at_stake: When fine-tuning makes a model forget, the knowledge is erased: what the model says is what it has.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: Du 2025: frozen base truth probe works on the instruct model (within ±4 points), but the answers were never degraded. Zhang, Choshen & Andreas 2024: forgetting to chance with knowledge still decodable, but by a probe retrained after. Never combined.

directions.title: Source lost before content: when a model's conversations are consolidated into its weights, does it keep what was said but lose who said it?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: the in-context gate probably passes (roles are labelled); content d' >= 0.5 after a small LoRA on 4-bit is uncertain; content d' in context may sit near ceiling above source d', so the difference-of-drops rule has a ceiling problem; familiarity of own items blurs both measures.
directions.assumption_at_stake: Weight-based memory for LLM agents (consolidating conversations into LoRA weights) keeps the model's record of which content was its own commitment and which came from the user.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: People lose source before content (Johnson 1993). LLMs: source measured in context only (Ranjan 2026: own items 38% vs user items 76% after a delay); consolidation into weights measured for retention only (Spens & Burgess 2026; Dennis 2026); CCOPD says its test is not role-matched. No read measures source after consolidation.
directions.what_our_data_say: On Haiku, a number framed as the model's own answer pulls its re-rating and another person's ~0: own minus other +0.46 [+0.21, +0.84] (results/bm0-source-distance-lag.md); hidden own answer: repeat consistency 86% -> 36%. Not run on Llama.
directions.cheapest_test: Llama-3-8B-4bit: word-pair transcripts, half model-generated, half user-given; gate on in-context source d'; LoRA SFT on the full transcripts; then, without the transcript, source d' and content recognition d'.
directions.odds_event: Gate: in-context source d' >= 1.0, and content recognition d' after consolidation >= 0.5. PASS if the drop in source d' from in-context to consolidated exceeds the drop in content d' (difference > 0, item-bootstrap 95% interval above 0).
directions.question: If a model's conversations are trained into its memory, does it keep what was said but lose track of who said it?
known: People keep content and lose its source as memories age; models in context lose track of their own items after a delay (Ranjan 2026).
Our own finding: Claude treats its own earlier answer as a commitment and someone else's as nearly nothing. Nobody has checked this after memories are trained in.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth most of a day of laptop time (free) to find out whether a model that has its conversations trained into its memory keeps what was said but loses track of who said it, itself or the user? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it loses who-said-it faster than what-was-said)?
engine_only: the in-context gate (source d' >= 1.0) passes on Llama-3-8B: engine odds 0.75 (scout, one pass, not v1)
directions.prior_work_line: Human source-monitoring predicts a pass: Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay 1993 (Psych. Bull. 114:3) report content kept and source lost with delay. In LLMs, Ranjan, Sokratous and Odegaard 2026 (arXiv:2607.23927; six open models, in context only) found own items sourced worse than user items after a delay (38% vs 76% in the repo read). No paper measures source after consolidation into weights; Dennis 2026 (arXiv:2605.24657) measured retention only. Not Claude.

directions.title: Consolidation dissolves the order effect: if a model's own answer is distilled into its weights, does question order stop moving it?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: Llama showed order effects on only 3 of 10 items, projecting ~6 per half of 20 against a gate of 8, so the gate most likely fails; if it passes, a 50% drop is plausible, but noise (SD ~13 vs spans 20-30) and a 20-item bootstrap make the difference-in-differences hard to clear.
directions.assumption_at_stake: Question-order effects in LLM ratings are built at ask time from context; anchoring the judgment in the weights makes it resistant.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: Nearly run: SARA (Yu 2026, abstract only) self-distilled judges to be less sensitive to rubric order; CCOPD cut the pull of earlier turns. Open only for graded credences under sub-question order permutation.
directions.what_our_data_say: Haiku: ~25-point median order swing; hiding earlier answers leaves it about the same (R = 1.23 [0.75, 2.02]). Llama-3-8B: significant on 3 of 10 items, within-order SD ~13.
directions.cheapest_test: Llama-3-8B, 40 experiment-5 items: reverse-KL self-distillation of the bare-question rating on 20 random items; re-measure chain-order spans on trained vs held-out items.
directions.odds_event: Gate: >= 8 items per half show an order effect before training. PASS if the median order span on trained items falls by >= 50% and by more than on held-out items (difference in differences, item-bootstrap 95% interval above 0).
directions.question: If a model's own answer is trained into its memory, does the order of earlier questions stop moving it?
known: Similar training already made AI judges less sensitive to the order of their checklists (SARA, 2026).
On the laptop model the order effect is weak and noisy (3 of 10 items), so the test may not get off the ground.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth most of a day of laptop time (free) to find out whether training a model's own answer into its memory stops the order of earlier questions from moving that answer? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means order moves the trained answers at most half as much as before, and less than the untrained ones)?
engine_only: the gate (>= 8 items per half with an order effect) passes on Llama-3-8B: engine odds 0.30 (scout, one pass, not v1)

Lin et al. 2026 (CCOPD, arXiv:2605.30251; Qwen3-8B) cut the pull of the model's own earlier turns (33.0 to 89.3). Neither permutes sub-question order. Not Claude.

directions.odds_template: v1
directions.title: Retrieval-induced forgetting in the weights: does practising recall of some facts make a model forget their neighbours?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: interference is plausible (fine-tuning damages related facts; practised exemplars may crowd the cue), but shared representations may help instead; only 12 Rp- items against 24 Nrp, so the bootstrap interval clears 0 only for a large drop; stage 1's 80% floor leaves little room.
directions.assumption_at_stake: In gradient-trained networks, practising some items of a category helps or is neutral for the rest; the human 'remembering causes forgetting' effect is not a property of weights.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: People: 37.5% vs 48.4% (Anderson 1994); g = 0.22 with output order controlled (Murayama 2014). LLMs: in context only, Qwen-2.5-7B +11.2 pp (Li & Wang 2026). In weights: not found; knowledge-editing literature not read.
directions.what_our_data_say: Nothing direct; program 1 measured judgments, not recall.
directions.cheapest_test: LoRA stage 1 teaches 8 fictional categories x 6 exemplars to >= 80% cued recall; stage 2 retrieval practice on 3 exemplars in 4 categories; then cued recall of all, unpractised items of practised categories first. Size categories from a pilot.
directions.odds_event: PASS if cued recall of unpractised items in practised categories (Rp-) is lower than of items in unpractised categories (Nrp) by >= 5 percentage points, item-bootstrap 95% interval above 0, with Rp- items tested first.
directions.question: Does drilling a model on some facts make it forget related facts it was not drilled on, the way it happens to people?
known: It happens to people, though the effect is small once done carefully, and it happens in a model's short-term context (Li & Wang 2026).
Nobody has checked it in a model's trained memory.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few hours of laptop time (free) to find out whether drilling a model on some facts makes it forget related facts it wasn't drilled on, the way it happens to people? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the related, undrilled facts are recalled clearly worse)?
engine_only: the in-context version replicates on Llama-3-8B (>= 5 pp): engine odds 0.45 (scout, one pass, not v1)
directions.prior_work_line: Prediction by analogy only. People: Anderson, Bjork and Bjork 1994 (JEP:LMC 20:1063) 37.5% vs 48.4%; Murayama et al. 2014 meta-analysis g = 0.22 with output order controlled. LLMs in context: Li and Wang 2026 (ICML 2026 FAGEN workshop poster; Qwen-2.5-7B and 72B) found elaboration on one set cut recall of related items by 11.2 and 24.9 points. Nothing found with retrieval practice in the weights. Not Claude.

Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli, Storm 2014, Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analysis, Psychological Bulletin 140(5)

directions.odds_template: v1
directions.short: A closing turn clears order effects
directions.title: The order effect as interference: does a mock 'those questions are finished' turn stop earlier questions moving the model's answer?
directions.odds_rationale: Fresh v1 context: the gate is probably met (~12 of 40 projected), but our redaction data say the effect comes from the questions themselves, so one closing sentence is unlikely to halve the span; repeat noise (SD ~13, 10 repeats) puts a floor under the span; Wang's gains were in key-value retrieval, not ratings.
directions.assumption_at_stake: The question-order effect is a judgment built from the whole question history, not interference from earlier items that an event boundary could clear.
directions.who_looked_and_why_open: Wang 2025: a mock closing QA turn helps LLMs escape proactive interference in key-value tracking, a 'forget' instruction gains < 10 pp; Chattaraj 2026: proactive beats retroactive interference in all 39 LLMs. Neither touched graded judgments or order effects.
directions.what_our_data_say: Haiku: ~25-point median order swing; hiding earlier answers leaves it about the same size (question-driven). Llama-3-8B: order effect on 3 of 10 items, within-order SD ~13.
directions.cheapest_test: Llama-3-8B-4bit, 40 experiment-5 items, chains O1-O4, one scale, 10 repeats, with vs without a mock closed QA turn before the main question.
directions.odds_event: Gate: >= 8 items show an order effect without the reset. PASS if the median order span with the reset is <= 50% of the span without it (item-bootstrap 95% interval of the ratio below 1), while the no-chain baseline rating moves <= 5 points.
directions.question: Does telling the model 'those questions are finished, here is a new one' stop earlier questions from moving its answer?
known: Models struggle to ignore earlier information, and a turn that closes it off helps them in memory tasks (Wang 2025).
Our own data say the order effect comes from the questions themselves, which a closing line may not clear.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a couple of hours of laptop time (free) to find out whether telling the model 'those questions are finished, here is a new one' stops the earlier questions from moving its answer? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it cuts the effect of question order at least in half)?
directions.prior_work_line: Wang and Sun 2025 (arXiv:2506.08184, ICML 2025 LCFM workshop; key-value tracking, 30-plus models) found instructions to ignore earlier input give limited gains, while in the repo's read a mock closing QA turn helped substantially; that predicts the pass direction for retrieval accuracy, not graded ratings. Chattaraj and Raj 2026 (arXiv:2603.00270; 39 models including Claude 4.5) show proactive interference dominates in context. No prior test on order effects.
prior_work_sources: Wang, Sun 2025, Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length, arXiv:2506.08184
Chattaraj, Raj 2026, LLMs remember first, forget last: dual-process interference, arXiv:2603.00270 (repo read)

directions.title: Self-generated ('dreamed') vs real vs no replay in LLM continual fine-tuning
directions.diagnosis: Already run: LAMOL (GPT-2) and self-synthesized rehearsal on Llama-2-7B LoRA (BWT -42.39 none, -3.02 real, -0.79 self-synthesized); in vision, stored replay beats generative (GDumb). Only new outcome measures would add anything, and those are in bmq-d1 and bmq-d2.

directions.title: Sleep-like synaptic downscaling: shrink the fine-tuning delta toward the base model between tasks
directions.diagnosis: Nearly run (WiSE-FT on CLIP; Mirzadeh 2020; quantization rounding restores old knowledge, Zhang 2024) and confounded: shrinking a delta trades learning for retention by construction (Subramanian 2026, abstract). The informative version is a learning-strength-matched method comparison with no stake in an assumption about minds.

directions.title: Selective ('triage') replay of uncertain or tagged items
directions.diagnosis: Already run: surprise-prioritised replay on Llama-3.1-8B (SuRe, 68.53 vs 50.53 random). Human prior small after bias correction (targeted reactivation g = 0.13). Our variant has no assumption at stake.

directions.title: Forgotten knowledge resurfaces; relearning savings; spacing
directions.diagnosis: Run many times on 7-8B models (Deeb & Roger; Hu; Lynch; Zheng; Jain; Kotha; Jiang; Yang 2024 anticipatory recovery). Kept only as a secondary recovery arm of bmq-d1.

directions.title: Sleep-replay consolidation (Tadros 2022) on a transformer
directions.diagnosis: Not ours: the spiking-conversion and Hebbian method has no transformer version, so this is method work, not a test of a mind; evidence MLP/CNN only; no independent replication found.

directions.title: Mortal computation (Hinton 2022; Ororbia & Friston 2023)
directions.diagnosis: No test exists on an open-weight software model: mortal computation is defined by hardware-bound, non-copyable computation.

directions.title: Importance-weighted consolidation (EWC, synaptic intelligence, memory-aware synapses) on LoRA
directions.diagnosis: Method benchmarking in a crowded field, vision evidence only; simple baselines win under honest evaluation (Farquhar & Gal 2018; van de Ven & Tolias 2019); it asks nothing about a mind.

directions.title: Active forgetting by periodic embedding resets (Chen 2023)
directions.diagnosis: Needs pretraining scale, and is about plasticity for new languages, not retention.

directions.title: Gist and false memory (DRM lures) after consolidation into weights
directions.diagnosis: Nearly run: Spens & Burgess 2026 show semanticisation after LoRA consolidation on Mistral-7B; the human sleep and false-memory effect is null overall (g = 0.13, sign flips with list length).

directions.title: A reconsolidation window for LoRA edits (retrieve, then update)
directions.diagnosis: The human flagship (Schiller 2010) fails principled reanalysis (Chalkia 2020); the knowledge-editing literature was not read; the prediction is worth little.

directions.title: Consolidation protects against interference (A-B in weights, A-C in context)
directions.diagnosis: Does not transfer cleanly: with A-B in weights and A-C in context, the 'correct' answer is set by the question, which is the knowledge-conflict literature (not read), not interference.

directions.title: Facts consistent with the model's priors are learned faster and interfere less (Kumaran 2016)
directions.diagnosis: Probably run in the LLM knowledge-injection literature (not read here; named for a later scout).

directions.title: Fan effect in LLM memory
directions.diagnosis: Not about forgetting, and Llama-3 showed no reliable effect (Roberts 2024).

directions.title: Gold map 7: two-friend local friendliness with external settings on ibm_fez
directions.prior_work_line: Quantum theory predicts a violation; hardware has shown only weaker forms. directions.short: Entangled claims: quantum walk vs PageRank
directions.title: Sean's entangled-claims idea: does a quantum walk over program 1's claim graph predict which of its directions were killed and which hit, better than PageRank does?
directions.engine_odds_em_qwalk2_note: lesson ls-em-qwalk2: labels planted from the quantum kernel pass the re-bet rule only 1-2%, shuffled labels 0.1-0.4% (programs/entangled-mind/experiments/qwalk2.md section 4)

directions.odds_event: On program 1's claim graph (the directions in map/entangled-mind.json as nodes, parent links and shared-data/replication links as edges), a continuous-time quantum walk started from the known hits and kills, scored leave-one-node-out, predicts each resolved node's outcome (hit 1, killed 0; mixed and open left out) with AUROC higher than personalised PageRank on the same graph and the same seeds, by a bootstrap 95% interval whose lower end is above 0. Quantum counts only if it beats this classical baseline; beating chance alone does not count.

Lower again because about 25 labelled nodes on a near-tree give little power, and on a tree a quantum walk's ranking and a diffusion's are close. Odds are for beating PageRank, not for beating chance.
directions.question: Can the way program 1's ideas connect to each other, treated as a quantum system, tell which of them were going to fail, better than ordinary link-ranking can?
known: Program 1's quantum-against-classical tests: the classical twin matched or won all six.
The claim graph and every outcome are already in the ledger, so the test costs nothing; the quantum walk is simulated on the laptop, no chip.

Pre-register the walk time, the PageRank damping and the edge list before the outcomes are joined.
directions.cost: $0 API; laptop minutes; no chip time (the walk is a simulation, invariant 9)
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few minutes of laptop time (free) to treat program 1's ideas as a connected quantum system, and see whether that tells which ideas were going to fail better than ordinary link-ranking (the way search engines rank pages) does? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the quantum version beats ordinary link-ranking, not just chance)?

A 2023) found a continuous-time quantum-walk link predictor performs similarly to classical path-based predictors on real networks in simulation. Paparo et al. 2013 (Sci. Rep. 3:2773, arXiv:1303.3891) found quantum PageRank changes the node hierarchy and resolves ties on scale-free graphs, with no accuracy benchmark against outcomes. directions.title: Does Opus's own stated confidence flag its wrong answers, as Haiku's and Sonnet's do?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The error signal in stated confidence is a property of the smaller models only.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only: em-dm3 holds Opus's answers with its stated confidence and correctness; score how well confidence separates right from wrong (AUROC, item bootstrap).
directions.models: archive: Opus's own archived answers (Haiku and Sonnet already scored in phase A and em-gm1)
directions.odds_event: Opus's stated confidence on its own answers separates its errors with AUROC >= 0.75, 95% item-bootstrap interval above 0.5.
directions.odds_rationale: Stated confidence was the best error signal on Haiku (0.82) and Sonnet (0.91); stronger models are usually at least as well calibrated in ranking. directions.title: Does the pull toward the last rating have the human serial-dependence shape, largest at middling gaps?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The model's pull toward its previous rating is a simple linear anchor, not the tuned pull seen in human perception.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only: bm9's Haiku conversations; fit the pull against the gap between ratings, a derivative-of-Gaussian against a straight line, by AIC.
directions.odds_event: A derivative-of-Gaussian fit beats a linear fit by delta-AIC >= 4, with its peak inside the observed range of gaps.
directions.odds_rationale: Human serial dependence has this shape, but a language model has no perceptual tuning, and a linear anchor is the simpler account; the archive's range of gaps may be too narrow to see a peak. Well below the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
